title: Log
text:
30 August 2026 · Defining Openended learning
Link: This paper helped clarify what actually counts as open-ended learning.
An open-ended process should continue producing novel elements over an indefinite horizon. These elements could be:

observations
options
reward functions
goals
skills

The important part is the combination of:

novelty
continued production
no fixed endpoint

Intrinsic motivation feels important because it gives the agent internal reasons to keep exploring rather than only following an external reward.
From the agent’s perspective, this could look like:

Have I seen this before?
Did reality surprise my model?
Am I getting better at this?
Is this behaviour different from my other behaviours?
Is this a new achievable outcome?

This feels similar to natural-computing ideas: maintain diversity and explore alternatives rather than only optimise one fixed goal.
The difficult part is deciding what kind of diversity is actually useful. Maximising divergence alone could produce lots of different but pointless behaviours. An open-ended agent probably needs diversity as a navigation mechanism, while still favouring discoveries that create useful building blocks for future learning.
The tension is that focusing only on building on what is already useful may trap the system in one local direction. It is like optimising the same square building for maximum height forever: eventually, progress may require discovering a completely different architecture rather than improving the current one.


28 August 2026 · Open-ended learning session
Q2: Branching. High-entropy points in generation could be used to deliberately fork reasoning, run alternative paths, and compare outcomes. Most of the branching machinery already exists. The interesting gap may be using branches to study strategic differences between agents, rather than only finding the correct answer.
Q1: What should an agent learn next? H-GRAIL showed a useful approach to autonomous goal discovery: existing skills can help an agent reach new states and discover further goals. For language agents, the harder problem is deciding whether a textual outcome represents something worth learning.
Q3: Internal reasoning. RecursiveMAS made the distinction clearer: latent communication is not interpretability. This raised a more specific question: does internal divergence happen before textual divergence? If not, the idea can be dropped.
Open-ended learning. The bigger issue is whether the current questions are actually open-ended. A fixed set of problems can test Q1–Q4 and eventually finish. Open-ended learning needs a continuing process where new things emerge over time.
Three missing elements.

Task supply / goal: new things to learn.
Persistence: discoveries survive over time or can be built upon.
Time: capability develops over an extended process.

Emerging thesis direction. A possible direction is a population of agents that develops complementary specialisations and uses them to discover capabilities that a single agent would not. The important word is self-organise.
Domain thoughts. Maths is useful for controlled measurement. Code may be better for genuinely open-ended generation. Science is compelling but difficult to verify. A useful domain may have limited variables but uncapped combinations.
Test. If an intelligent agent can finish it, it is probably a benchmark rather than an open-ended domain.

title: Q1: Knowing what to learn
text:
Q1: How does an agent decide what to learn next?
An agent dropped into an environment it knows nothing about it. It’s got to work out what is possible before it can know what is worth getting good at. It must keep switching between finding out what it can do and getting better at what it has already found.



Conceptual example. Imagine someone is given a cup with an unfamiliar shape. Their first attempt to hold it follows previous experience, but the interaction feels different. Nothing failed. The cup was picked up. What triggers exploration is that it did not go the way they expected, and that mismatch is enough to make them try it a few more ways.


The problem
The obvious answer to “what should I learn” is “whatever I just failed at”. That answer is wrong often enough to be a problem. A failure can mean three different things:

The agent cannot do it. Real gap, worth learning.
The agent can do it but took a bad route this time. Nothing is missing.
There is nothing to learn. The task is random or has no stable answer.



Working assumptions

An agent can notice when the environment responded differently from what it expected, even when nothing went wrong.
An effect the agent has caused once can be turned into something it aims for on purpose.
Skills already acquired can be used to reach situations where further discovery is possible.
Whether to explore or to practise is itself a decision the agent can make, rather than a schedule set in advance.



Open questions

How can an agent tell a real gap from a bad attempt, and both from something that cannot be learned at all?
What is the signal that something interesting has happened, for an agent working in text, code or a browser rather than one with a camera? (robotics)
When should the agent stop looking around and start practising, and what makes it switch back?
How does it decide that an effect it has just caused is genuinely new, rather than something it already knows how to do?



Getting out of the circle
H-GRAIL handles the bootstrapping problem in a way that seems repeatable outside robotics. 1. Its goal set starts empty’

“go and find out what is possible”
the agent can choose to do, sitting alongside “get better at what I already know” and a selector switches between the two.

It notices new goals by watching for changes in what it can see: press a button, the button lights up, that change becomes a goal it can now aim for on purpose. And it chooses where to start exploring based on which starting points have previously led to finding something new, so it uses skills it already has to put itself somewhere worth exploring from.
The loop that results:
knows nothing
     |
     v
acts without a goal  ->  the environment changes
     |
     v
that change becomes something it can aim for
     |
     v
learns to cause it reliably
     |
     v
uses that skill to reach places it could not reach before
     |
     v
explores from there  ->  new changes  ->  new goals
     |
     v
repeat, each round starting further out
The agent does not need to know what it can do before it starts. It needs one thing it can do and a way to notice when the environment responds.


What is missing for language agents
A robot gets its novelty signal for free: the pixels.
An agent working in text, code or a browser gets back a string and has to decide for itself whether anything meaningful occurred. There is no equivalent primitive, and that is the gap this question is aimed at.
Two related findings make it look worth pursuing. Training an agent purely to complete tasks does not produce an agent that explores well, and the resulting narrow behaviour hurts it later. And when a language model proposes its own tasks without having interacted with the environment, it produces a lot of tasks that are impossible and a lot that the agent can already do, because it has no grounding in either the environment or its own current ability.


Scope note
Two things get run together under “discovering what it can do” and this question separates them. The set of actions the agent can attempt is normally fixed and given. What grows is the set of effects it knows it can bring about, and that set has no ceiling because effects combine. This question is about the second. It does not claim the agent invents new primitive actions.


Supporting literature and concepts
Open-ended learning; intrinsic motivation; competence progress and learning progress; novelty and curiosity; goal discovery.


Related papers

A Motivational Architecture for Open-Ended Learning Challenges in Robots (H-GRAIL) starts from an empty goal set and makes goal discovery a motivation the agent can select, alongside improving at goals it has already found.
Look Before You Leap: Autonomous Exploration for LLM Agents introduces a measure of how much of an unfamiliar environment an agent actually discovers, and finds that training for task completion does not produce agents that explore.
Automated Skill Discovery for Language Agents through Exploration and Iterative Feedback shows why letting a model propose its own tasks without grounding produces tasks that are either impossible or already solved.
Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models pairs a self-generated curriculum with a growing library of skills stored as code for reuse.
EvolveR: Self-Evolving LLM Agents through Experience studies how agents turn experience into strategies they can reuse later.
SoK: Agentic Skills — Beyond Tool Use in LLM Agents surveys the area and notes that fully autonomous discovery is still rare, since most systems rely on a human to define what counts as progress.



Why this matters for the rest of the work
Nothing else starts until something decides there is a problem worth working on. If the tasks are handed to the system, this question does not arise and the work stops being open-ended: the Navigator becomes a measurement tool applied to a fixed dataset with a fixed ceiling. This question is what keeps the tasks moving as the system gets better.
Status: Exploring

title: Q3: Reasoning pathways
text:
Q3: Can the internal states of an agent show where its reasoning diverged?
Two agents running the same model on the same task end up reasoning differently. That difference is visible in what they write. The question is whether it is visible inside them first, and whether the inside view says anything the text does not.





The question, sharpened
Q2 compares two pieces of reasoning by what the model said. That works, it is cheap, and it needs no access to the model’s insides. This question asks whether opening the model up is worth the extra cost:

Does the divergence show up in the internal states before it shows up in the text?

If the answer is no, then internal states are a more expensive way of seeing something the words already showed, and this question can be closed. If the answer is yes, then the model commits to an approach before it writes anything that reveals it, and there is a whole layer the text-level view cannot reach.
Everything else on this page depends on that one result, so it is worth settling early.


Why it might be yes
Two reasons to expect the inside view to show more:

A model does not always write down what actually drove its answer. If that is true, comparing what two agents wrote compares their explanations, not their reasoning.
And if there is a line of work where agents pass hidden states to each other instead of text. In that setting the reasoning never becomes words at all. If systems keep moving in that direction, reading internal states stops being optional.



Working assumptions

Activations can be recorded from any model whose weights are available. Size limits how much can be stored and how easily it can be interpreted.
Two agents running the same base model produce states in the same coordinate space, so their internal states can be compared directly.
Agents running different models do not share a coordinate space, and comparing them needs a method built for that
Some part of a model’s internal state carries which approach it is taking, seprate from what it produces (shows)



Open questions

Does internal divergence come before textual divergence, and by how much?
Which states are worth recording: residual stream, attention patterns, or something learned on top of them?
Can two agents running different models be compared at all, or only two copies of the same one?
Is there anything in the internal state that says an approach is going to fail, before the failure appears in the output?



Available methods
Some tools already exist and are not specific to this question.

Projecting intermediate states onto the vocabulary to see what the model is leaning toward mid-computation.
Training small probes to test whether a given property is present in a state.
Sparse autoencoders for pulling apart states that mix many things at once.
Attention analysis for which earlier parts of the text a later part is drawing on.
Representational similarity methods for comparing across models that do not share a coordinate space.

Note. Thought Anchors already asks this from both sides. From the outside it rewinds to a step, runs the model again many times, and sees whether the answer changes: if it does, that step was a real decision. From the inside it blocks the model from looking back at that step and sees what breaks. Same question, once from the words and once from the machinery, which is the comparison this page is built on.


Possible investigation
Reuse the branching set-up from Q2 rather than building a new one. For each fork point, record the internal states in the run-up to it as well as the branches that follow.
Then ask three things in order:

Do the internal states shortly before a fork predict which branch gets taken?
Do they predict whether that branch succeeds, earlier than the text does?
If yes to either, how far ahead of the words does the signal appear?



Scope note
This is the same measurement problem as Q2 with a different instrument. Q2 asks whether two pieces of reasoning are doing the same thing, judged from the output. Q3 asks the same, judged from the inside. It is deliberately the second instrument to build, because the cheap one should be shown to be insufficient before the expensive one is justified.


Related papers

Recursive Multi-Agent Systems
Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter? pairs text-level resampling with attention-based attribution and attention suppression
Hybrid Latent Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning works on reasoning carried in hidden states rather than in a written chain of thought.
See What I See, Know What I Think: Dense Latent Communication Across Heterogeneous Agents covers latent communication between agents built on different models.

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text: How can generative AI agents support personalised active learning by adapting educational experiences to individual students while providing teachers with meaningful insights into student understanding?

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text:
Student Agent Role
Each student agent builds an evolving model of the student’s learning process by analysing interactions such as:

answers and mistakes
homework and activity completion
engagement patterns
reasoning and explanations
confidence and uncertainty

The goal is not to diagnose students, but to identify learning patterns, misconceptions, and areas where additional support may be needed.

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text:
Teacher Intelligence Agent
A teacher-level agent aggregates information from student agents and provides higher-level insights.
Instead of manually reviewing individual interactions, the teacher receives summaries of:

common misconceptions
students requiring additional support
engagement changes
learning progress

The teacher remains responsible for deciding interventions.

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text:
Potential Applications

Early identification of learning difficulties
Personalised support recommendations
Classroom-level learning insights
Evaluation of learning activities

title: Agent Systems
text:
An AI agent is a system that uses a large language model (LLM) as a reasoning component combined with tools, memory, and feedback mechanisms to achieve goals autonomously.
Unlike a traditional LLM application:
Input → Model → Output
An agent operates through an iterative loop where it can observe, reason, act, and update its state.
flowchart LR
Goal[Goal] --> Observe[Observe Environment]
Observe --> Reason[Reason / Plan]
Reason --> Act[Take Action]
Act --> Feedback[Evaluate Result]
Feedback --> Memory[Update State / Memory]
Memory --> Observe
The key difference is that an agent can decide actions, use tools, maintain state, and adapt based on feedback.

State
Track task progress


Evaluation

title: Q2: Divergent reasoning
text:
Component: Navigator - finds the points where the reasoning could have gone another way, and checks whether the different routes are genuinely different approaches.







Q2: Why do identical agents develop different reasoning strategies?
This note investigates whether branching at high-entropy decision points can create genuinely different reasoning strategies, rather than only different phrasings or final outcomes. The agent takes one route. Then it goes back and runs the routes it didn’t take, and learns from those. It learns from things it never did.



Procedure.

One agent produces a complete reasoning trace and a final answer. This is the reference trace.
The token-level entropy of the reference trace is recorded, and the highest-entropy positions are identified as candidate decision points.
At each decision point, generation is resumed from the preceding prefix with a different continuation, and each branch is run to completion.
The outcomes of the branches are compared against the outcome of the reference trace. A decision point is important if resampling it changes the distribution over final answers. This is its counterfactual point
Where the reference trace failed and its branches succeed, the decision point marks where the reasoning went wrong. That position, and the continuation that recovered from it, can be recorded for reuse.

Working assumptions for this mechanism.

High-entropy positions correspond to meaningful choices in the reasoning rather than to surface variation in wording.
Failure in a reasoning trace can be localised to a small number of positions rather than being distributed across the whole trace.
The alternative continuations produced at a decision point represent different strategies, not different phrasings of the same strategy.

Open questions for this mechanism.

Do branches taken at the same decision point differ in strategy, or only in outcome?
What distinguishes a decision point that produces a useful alternative from one that produces an equivalent restatement?
How should a recorded failure point be abstracted so that it transfers to a different problem, rather than being tied to the trace it came from?
Which level is the right unit of branching: the token, the sentence, or the reasoning step?

Scope note. This mechanism addresses only the first source of divergence listed above, stochasticity. It says nothing about divergence arising from experience, memory, or communication. It also operates on the model’s output distribution rather than its internal representations; the internal version of the same question is Q3.
Supporting literature and concepts. Token entropy and forking tokens; entropy-guided decoding and branching; counterfactual importance and step-level attribution; tree search over reasoning traces.
Related papers.

Beyond the 80/20 Rule: High-Entropy Minority Tokens Drive Effective Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning establishes that a small minority of tokens carry most of the branching behaviour in a chain of thought, and that these tokens act as forks steering the model toward different reasoning pathways.
Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter? measures the counterfactual importance of each sentence in a reasoning trace by resampling from that position, .and finds that planning and uncertainty-management steps matter more than computation steps.
ETTRL: Balancing Exploration and Exploitation in LLM Test-Time Reinforcement Learning implements fork-based exploration at high-entropy tokens and reuses the low-entropy segments between forks.
Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology tests how changing agent communication structures affects collective reasoning.

Possible investigation: Take one open-weights reasoning model and a set of problems with checkable answers. Generate a reference trace per problem, record token entropy, branch at the highest-entropy positions, and run each branch to a final answer. Then cluster the branches by strategy rather than by correctness, and ask whether branching at a decision point produces genuinely distinct approaches or only distinct wordings of one approach.
                 Reference trace
                        |
        low entropy ----+---- low entropy
                        |
                 decision point
            ------------+------------
            |           |           |
        branch A    branch B    branch C
            |           |           |
            v           v           v
         outcome     outcome     outcome
            |           |           |
            ------------+------------
                        v
          Counterfactual importance of
              this decision point
                        v
           Strategy comparison across
                     branches
Why this matters for the rest of the work. This experiment does not answer a question on its own. If I want a group of agents that each do something different, I first need a way to tell whether two agents are actually doing different things, or just saying the same thing in different words. There is no agreed way to do that for reasoning yet. Working out how to group reasoning traces by approach is that tool. Once I have it, I can give each branch its own memory and follow it across many problems (Q2), keep a store of different approaches rather than only the best-scoring one, and pass approaches between agents to see if they transfer (Q4).
Status: Exploring

title: Q4: Capability accumulation
text:
Q4: How can capabilities accumulate across agents?
If one agent discovers a useful capability, that capability may be transferable to another agent, combinable with other capabilities, and reusable to produce something new.



Working assumptions.

Agents can represent useful capabilities in a form that another agent can use.
Shared memory, communication, or social learning can preserve and transfer those capabilities.
Combining capabilities can produce new behaviour rather than only copying existing behaviour.

Open questions.

Under what conditions can a population of agents accumulate capabilities over time?
How can transferred capabilities be combined without losing what made them useful?
What would show that the collective system has developed beyond the capability of an individual agent?

Supporting literature and concepts. Multi-agent learning; social learning; shared memory; Recursive Multi-Agent Systems; Evolver; cumulative capability growth.
Related paper. This question is closely related to Recursive Multi-Agent Systems, which examines recursive multi-agent reasoning and latent-space communication.
Current direction. Explore whether a population of agents can continually develop beyond the capabilities of its individual members.
Status: Exploring

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
Do LLM agents cooperate or defect when placed in a repeated strategic interaction — without being told what game they are playing?
This experiment sets up two teams of agents in a repeated two-choice environment. The agents are given neutral labels (option_a and option_b) and are never told the payoff structure is a prisoner’s dilemma. The goal is to observe whether cooperation emerges, and how team discussion affects decision-making.






Note



Source code and full results: github.com/1dzl0/agent-game

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
Payoff Matrix
Each round, both teams independently choose option_a or option_b. Rewards are determined by the combination of both teams’ choices.




Team B: option_a
Team B: option_b




Team A: option_a
3, 3
0, 5


Team A: option_b
5, 0
1, 1



This is the classic prisoner’s dilemma structure:

Mutual cooperation (A, A) → both score 3 — best joint outcome
Mutual defection (B, B) → both score 1 — worst joint outcome
Unilateral defection → defector scores 5, cooperator scores 0

Agents see only “option_a” and “option_b” in their prompts. The payoff values are revealed through the history of rounds, not upfront.

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
Agent Architecture
Each team has multiple agents. Before each round, agents share private messages within their team, then each agent votes independently. The team’s final action is determined by majority vote.





flowchart TD
    GS[Game State\npublic history + scores] --> OA[Observation Builder]
    TH[Private Team History] --> OA

    OA --> D1[Agent 1 Discussion]
    OA --> D2[Agent 2 Discussion]

    D1 -->|private message| TV[Team Vote]
    D2 -->|private message| TV

    TV --> DA1[Agent 1\nDecision]
    TV --> DA2[Agent 2\nDecision]

    DA1 -->|vote| MV[Majority Vote]
    DA2 -->|vote| MV

    MV --> TA[Team Action]
    TA --> RM[Reward\nCalculation]
    RM --> GS

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
What agents are told
Agents receive a prompt like this each round — no mention of game theory, prisoner’s dilemma, or strategic naming:

Your team score: 6.

Public history:
Round 1: team_alpha selected option_a, team_beta selected option_a. team_alpha received 3 points, team_beta received 3 points.
Round 2: team_alpha selected option_a, team_beta selected option_a. team_alpha received 3 points, team_beta received 3 points.

Private team channel:
team_alpha_agent_1: ...
team_alpha_agent_2: ...

The available choices are option_a and option_b.
